sections.body: Artificial intelligence in medicine is the use of pattern recognition, language models and simulation to support decisions that were once made entirely by clinicians. In radiology it flags suspicious regions on scans and sorts worklists by urgency, while in genomics it helps interpret variants and match patients to targeted therapies. Ambient documentation systems listen to a consultation and draft the clinical note, and triage tools rank incoming patients by predicted need. Drug discovery programs use models to propose molecules and predict binding before anything is made in a lab. This site tracks 1000 medical AI models, which gives a sense of how broad the field has become across these ten areas.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The clearest progress is in narrow, well measured tasks such as image classification, note drafting and appointment triage, where the output is checked by a person before it matters. What is not solved is the long tail: rare presentations, patients who do not resemble the training data, and the messy handoffs between departments where most errors actually occur. Prediction models in intensive care often perform well in the hospital that built them and less well elsewhere, and the reasons are usually about data and workflow rather than the algorithm. Regulation is still catching up, and the site's 229 compliance and regulation pages reflect how much of the work now sits in documentation, audit and device security rather than modelling. There are 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which is a reminder that accountability questions are being settled in court as much as in guidance.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader new to the field should start with Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology, since imaging is where deployment is most mature and the lessons generalize. Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics and Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation cover the laboratory and discovery side, where timelines are longer and evidence is thinner. Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence, Telemedicine and Triage, and Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care describe tools that sit directly in the clinical workflow and raise the hardest questions about oversight. Surgical Robotics and Navigation and Neuroinformatics and the Brain cover the physical and the neuroscientific edges of the field, where the technology is impressive and the outcome data is still accumulating. Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security is the page to read alongside all of the others, because it explains who approves these systems, how they are monitored after release, and what happens when they fail.
